description: How new medicines are developed, tested and evaluated. Key concepts and applications explained.
content_html:
Why We Need New Medicines

Developing a new medicine is one of the longest and most expensive processes in science. From initial discovery to reaching patients, it can take more than a decade. Most candidate compounds fail somewhere along the way — they may prove toxic, ineffective, or only marginally better than existing treatments. Understanding the pipeline from laboratory to pharmacy shelf is important both scientifically and as a lesson in how evidence informs decisions.

Medicines work by interacting with specific biological targets — receptors, enzymes, or pathways — to alter the body’s response to disease. Before any new drug reaches a patient, it must pass through a series of testing stages designed to establish that it is safe and effective. These stages generate the evidence base that regulators and clinicians use to decide whether a drug should be approved.

Stage 1: Preclinical Testing

Preclinical testing is carried out in the laboratory before any human volunteers are involved. Candidate compounds are tested on cells grown in culture and on animal models. These tests look at whether the drug has any biological activity against the target, whether it is toxic to cells at the doses being considered, and how the body metabolises and eliminates it.

Preclinical testing narrows down a large number of candidates to a smaller set that appears promising enough to justify human trials. It does not guarantee safety in humans — human physiology differs from animal physiology in important ways — but it removes the most obviously dangerous or ineffective candidates before any person is put at risk.

Key Fact

Preclinical testing uses cells and animals to check a drug’s basic safety and biological activity before any human testing begins. It eliminates the most dangerous or ineffective candidates but cannot guarantee human safety.

Stage 2: Clinical Trials

Clinical trials test new drugs in human participants. They proceed in phases, each with a different goal. Early phases use small numbers of healthy volunteers to establish that the drug is safe and to find an effective dose range. Later phases involve larger groups of patients with the target disease to test whether the drug actually works.

Phase 1 — a small number of healthy volunteers (typically a few dozen). The aim is to test safety, identify side effects, and determine how the drug behaves in the human body (pharmacokinetics). Doses start very low and are gradually increased.

Phase 2 — a larger group of patients with the target condition (typically hundreds). The aim is to gain initial evidence of effectiveness and to refine the dosing. Researchers also continue monitoring safety.

Phase 3 — a large-scale trial involving many hundreds or thousands of patients, often across multiple hospitals and countries. The drug is compared against the current best treatment (or a placebo, if no treatment exists). This phase provides the main evidence used by regulators to decide on approval.

Post-approval surveillance (Phase 4) — once a drug is approved and in use, monitoring continues in the general population. This can detect rare side effects that were too uncommon to appear in clinical trials.

Placebo Controls and Blind Trials

A placebo is an inactive substance that looks and feels identical to the real drug. Using a placebo as a control is essential because patients who believe they are receiving treatment often report improvements in symptoms — this is the placebo effect. Without a placebo control, it is impossible to know whether any improvement is due to the drug itself or to the psychological expectation of getting better.

To prevent bias from influencing results, trials use blinding. In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who are administering the treatment know who is in which group. The allocation is randomised and the code is only broken after all data have been collected. This prevents both patients and doctors from unconsciously behaving differently based on their knowledge of who received the drug.

Key Fact

A placebo control allows the true drug effect to be separated from the placebo effect. In a double-blind trial, neither the patient nor the administering researcher knows who receives the drug — this removes bias from both reporting and administration. Randomisation ensures the groups are comparable.

Antibiotics and the Problem of Resistance

Antibiotics are medicines that kill or slow the growth of bacteria. They work by targeting structures or processes that bacteria have but human cells lack — for example, bacterial cell walls or particular enzymes. This selectivity is what makes them useful: they harm the pathogen without (ideally) harming the patient.

However, bacteria reproduce rapidly and can evolve resistance. Antibiotic resistance arises when random mutations give some bacterial cells a survival advantage against the drug. These bacteria survive, reproduce, and pass on the resistance. Over time, if antibiotics are overused or misused — for example, taken for viral infections, or not completed as prescribed — resistant strains become dominant in a population.

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a well-known example of a drug-resistant bacterium. It is resistant to many commonly used antibiotics, making infections difficult to treat. MRSA spreads most readily in environments where many people are in close contact and where antibiotic use is high — hospitals are a particular concern.

Reducing antibiotic resistance requires coordinated action: doctors prescribing antibiotics only when appropriate, patients completing their courses, and researchers developing new classes of antibiotics. The pipeline for new antibiotics has slowed in recent decades because the development costs are high and the commercial returns are lower than for drugs used long-term. This creates a genuine public health challenge that involves both scientific and economic decision-making.

Peer Review and Evaluating Drug Evidence

When clinical trial results are published, they are subject to peer review. Reviewers who were not involved in the trial examine the methodology, statistical analysis, and conclusions. They may identify flaws, request additional data, or reject the paper if the evidence is insufficient. Peer review does not guarantee a paper is correct — errors can still slip through — but it provides an important quality filter.

Evaluating drug evidence also involves considering conflict of interest. Research funded by a pharmaceutical company that manufactures the drug being tested may be subject to reporting bias — the tendency for positive results to be published more readily than negative ones. Independent replication by separate research groups, and access to full trial data (not just selected results), strengthens the evidence base considerably.

Key Fact

Peer review subjects scientific findings to scrutiny by independent experts before publication. Conflict of interest — especially industry funding — can introduce bias. Independent replication and full data access are important safeguards.
exam_tip_html: For questions about clinical trials, make sure you know the specific function of each design feature: the placebo eliminates the placebo effect, randomisation makes the groups comparable, and double-blinding removes bias from both the patient and the researcher. Extended-response questions often ask you to “evaluate the design of a study” — identify what was done well, what is missing, and how it could be improved. Avoid vague statements; link each point to why it matters for the reliability of the results.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • New drugs pass through preclinical testing (cells and animals) and then phased clinical trials before approval — the process is designed to establish safety and effectiveness at each stage.
  • Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trials are the gold standard for testing medicines because they minimise bias and allow the true drug effect to be measured.
  • Antibiotic resistance develops through natural selection when resistant mutations survive drug exposure — overuse and misuse accelerate this process, making it a major public health challenge.

practice_questions.text: Explain why preclinical testing cannot guarantee that a drug will be safe in humans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Human physiology differs from animal physiology [1]; effects observed in animal models or cell cultures may not replicate in the human body [1].
Secure: States that animals and humans are different, so results may not apply to humans.
Developing: Says animals are not humans.
Emerging: Says testing is done on animals.

practice_questions.text: A new antibiotic is tested in a clinical trial. Half the patients receive the antibiotic; half receive a placebo. Neither the patients nor the doctors administering treatment know who is in which group. Explain what type of trial this is and why this design is important.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies double-blind trial [1]; explains that neither patient nor researcher knows who is in which group, preventing bias in symptom reporting and administration [1]; placebo controls for the placebo effect so any improvement in the antibiotic group can be attributed to the drug [1].
Secure: Names double-blind [1]; explains one source of bias it removes [1].
Developing: States neither group knows, without explaining why this matters.
Emerging: Describes the design without linking it to reliability.

practice_questions.text: Describe how antibiotic resistance develops in a bacterial population over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Random mutation gives some bacteria a survival advantage against the antibiotic [1]; these bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring [1]; over time the resistant strain becomes dominant in the population [1].
Secure: Mutation leads to resistance [1]; resistant bacteria reproduce more [1].
Developing: States bacteria become resistant after exposure, without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Says bacteria get used to the antibiotic.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that results from a clinical trial funded by the company manufacturing the drug provide reliable evidence for its effectiveness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States trials can still be rigorous regardless of funding [1]; identifies conflict of interest as a genuine concern (company may benefit financially from positive results) [1]; reporting bias — positive results more likely to be published than negative ones [1]; peer review provides some protection [1]; independent replication by separate groups strengthens confidence [1]; balanced conclusion weighing evidence quality against potential bias [1].
Secure: Identifies conflict of interest [1]; one further valid evaluative point [1]; limited conclusion.
Developing: States company funding may be biased without explaining mechanism.
Emerging: Simply agrees or disagrees without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why antibiotics are not prescribed for viral infections such as influenza.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria by targeting bacterial structures; they have no effect on viruses (accept: viruses lack the structures that antibiotics target).

practice_questions.text: A clinical trial for a new pain-relief drug has 40 participants in total. Suggest two ways in which the reliability of the trial could be improved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two valid improvements: Increase the sample size (40 is very small) [1]; use a double-blind design if not already in place [1]; ensure randomisation of participants to drug/placebo groups [1]; extend the trial duration to detect long-term effects or delayed side effects [1]. (Accept any two.)

knowledge_checks.q: What is the main purpose of the placebo in a clinical trial?
options: To provide a second active treatment for comparison
To eliminate the placebo effect so the drug's true benefit can be measured
To reduce the cost of the trial
To test whether participants can detect the difference between treatments

knowledge_checks.q: Which stage of drug testing involves healthy human volunteers for the first time?
Antibiotic resistance arises through natural _____, where bacteria with mutations that allow them to survive the drug reproduce and pass on the resistance.
In a double-blind trial, neither the _____ nor the researchers know which participants are in the treatment group.
Match each term to its correct description.
right: Scrutiny of scientific findings by independent experts before publication
Testing a drug on cells and animals before human trials
An inactive substance given to a control group to separate drug effect from expectation

flashcard_questions.a: Testing a drug on cells and animals before any human trials, to check basic safety and biological activity.

flashcard_questions.q: Phase 1 clinical trial: who are the participants and what is the goal?
flashcard_questions.a: Healthy volunteers; goal is to establish safety and find an effective dose range.
Improvement in symptoms due to the expectation of receiving treatment, not the drug itself.
To ensure participants are allocated to groups by chance, making the groups comparable and reducing selection bias.
Neither participants nor the administering researchers know who receives the drug or placebo until the trial ends.

flashcard_questions.q: What are antibiotics and which pathogens do they target?
flashcard_questions.a: Medicines that kill or inhibit bacteria; they are not effective against viruses.
Random mutations give some bacteria survival advantage; these reproduce and pass on resistance through natural selection.

flashcard_questions.q: MRSA stands for _____ and is notable because ___.
flashcard_questions.a: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; it is resistant to many commonly used antibiotics.

flashcard_questions.q: What is peer review in science?
flashcard_questions.a: Scrutiny of scientific work by independent experts before publication, to check for errors and unsupported conclusions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is conflict of interest in drug research?
flashcard_questions.a: When a researcher or funder has a financial stake in the outcome, which may bias reporting of results.

flashcard_questions.q: What is reporting bias in clinical trials?
flashcard_questions.a: The tendency for positive results to be published more readily than negative ones, giving a distorted picture of a drug's effectiveness.

flashcard_questions.q: Phase 3 trial: what is its purpose?
flashcard_questions.a: To test the drug in a large patient population, comparing it against current treatment or placebo to provide the main evidence for regulatory approval.

glossary_terms.definition: A protein on or in a cell that a drug binds to in order to produce its effect, such as an enzyme or ion channel.
Testing a drug on cells, tissues and living organisms before any clinical trials begin, to assess basic safety and biological activity.
A controlled study of a new drug or treatment in human volunteers, designed to assess safety, optimal dosage and effectiveness.
An inactive substance or treatment, identical in appearance to the drug being tested, given to a control group to separate the true drug effect from the placebo effect.
A clinical trial design in which neither the participants nor the researchers administering the trial know which participants are receiving the drug and which are receiving the placebo.
A type of medicine that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria by targeting bacterial structures; not effective against viruses.
The ability of bacteria to survive exposure to an antibiotic that would previously have killed them, arising through natural selection acting on random mutations.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — a bacterial strain resistant to many common antibiotics, posing serious risk especially in hospital settings.
The process by which scientific work is scrutinised by independent experts before publication, to check for errors, methodological weaknesses, and unsupported conclusions.
